mainTopic: Gifts from a גוי to the מקדש, a non-Jew's תרומה, and using money promised to צדקה
overview: The גמרא finds two ברייתות that disagree about accepting a גוי's donation for בדק הבית. רבי יוחנן explains that we refuse at the start of building and accept at the end, though even then not a noticeable item like the raven-repelling spikes. רב יוסף challenges this from נחמיה, who took wood from the Persian king, and אביי answers that a government never backs out of its word. Next, רב rules that if a non-Jew separates תרומה without a Jew's intent, it needs גניזה because he may have meant it for Heaven. A ברייתא about a beam with God's Name on it seems to disagree, but the גמרא explains that the Name is mentioned only to teach that the rest of the beam is not holy. The last topic is a coin promised to צדקה. The owner may use it and replace it, for himself or for others. רבא argues that the wording of his promise, 'עלי' or 'הרי זו', makes no difference, and a ברייתא supports him. רב זביד credits the whole rule to רב, and a final ברייתא teaches that once the coin reaches the גבאי it may no longer be switched.

steps.title: Two ברייתות contradict about a גוי's donation
steps.stepSummary: One ברייתא says we accept a גוי's donation for בדק הבית, and another says we do not.
steps.simpleTranslation: One ברייתא teaches: if a גוי pledged a gift for the upkeep of the בית המקדש, we accept it from him. Another ברייתא teaches: we do not accept it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא puts two ברייתות side by side, and they seem to say opposite things about taking a גוי's donation for בדק הבית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both ברייתות talk about the exact same case, a גוי donating to בדק הבית. One says yes and one says no, so the גמרא needs some way to make them fit together.

keyTerms.meaning: One ברייתא teaches... and another teaches. This is the standard way the גמרא sets up two sources that contradict each other.
Upkeep and repair of the בית המקדש building
A voluntary gift or donation
A non-Jew

phrases.english: It was taught in one ברייתא:
A gentile who pledged a gift for Temple maintenance
we accept it from him,
and another ברייתא teaches: we do not accept it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic about donations from a גוי.
steps.kashyaTarget: The two ברייתות about accepting a גוי's donation to בדק הבית
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same case gets opposite rulings, so both ברייתות cannot be right as they stand.

steps.title: Beginning of the building versus the end
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן explains that the two ברייתות speak about different stages: the start of building and the end.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אילא said in the name of רבי יוחנן: There is no problem. This ברייתא is talking about the beginning, and that ברייתא is talking about the end.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן settles the contradiction by saying each ברייתא is talking about a different time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא that says 'we do not accept' is talking about the beginning, when the בית המקדש is first being built. The ברייתא that says 'we accept' is talking about the end, after it is already built. So the two do not really argue.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult. The opening words of an answer that removes a contradiction.
This one... that one. Used to assign each source to a different case.
At the beginning, when the בית המקדש is first being built
At the end, after the building is already standing

steps.confusionAlert: Watch which ברייתא goes with which time. 'Do not accept' goes with the BEGINNING, and 'accept' goes with the END.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי אִילָא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Ila said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan:
It is not difficult,
this one is at the beginning,
phrases.notes: 'This one' is the ברייתא that says we do NOT accept.

phrases.english: that one is at the end.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא, הָא בַּתְּחִילָּה, הָא בַּסּוֹף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction raised in step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: each source applies to a different stage of the building
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two ברייתות seemed to argue about the same situation.
steps.terutzMaskana: Refusing applies at the start of building, and accepting applies once the building is finished.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן's fuller rule about beginning and end
steps.stepSummary: Another report of רבי יוחנן's teaching supports the answer and adds details: at the start nothing is accepted, and at the end only an unnoticeable item is accepted.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבי אסי said in the name of רבי יוחנן: At the beginning, we do not accept even water and salt from them. At the end, we do not accept a noticeable item, but we do accept an item that is not noticeable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up step 2 by quoting a fuller version of the same teaching of רבי יוחנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This shows the beginning-and-end split really is רבי יוחנן's view. It also adds two new details. At the beginning, even tiny cheap things like water and salt are refused. At the end, accepting is not total: a 'noticeable' item is still refused, and only an item that does not stand out is accepted.

keyTerms.meaning: As he said. It brings a supporting source for what was just said.
Water and salt. An example of the smallest, cheapest things.
A defined or noticeable item, one that stands out as a separate thing
An item that does not stand out and blends in

steps.whyThisMatters: It narrows the 'we accept' ruling. Even after the building is finished, accepting a גוי's gift has a limit.

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי אַסִּי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: As Rabbi Asi said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan:
At the beginning, even water and salt
we do not accept from them.
At the end, a noticeable item we do not accept,
an item that is not noticeable we accept.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי אַסִּי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports step 2 and expands it with more detail.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יוחנן's split between the beginning and the end
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי אסי's report of רבי יוחנן's teaching

steps.title: What counts as a noticeable item?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for an example of a 'noticeable item'.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is a case of a noticeable item?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what exactly 'a noticeable item' means. This sets up רב יוסף's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 3 used the phrase 'a noticeable item' without explaining it. Here the גמרא asks for a concrete example so the rule can be put into practice.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What does it look like?

phrases.english: What is a case of a noticeable item?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the meaning of a term used in step 3.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A concrete example of a דבר המסויים

steps.title: Example: the raven-repelling spikes
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף gives an example: the cubit of spikes on the roof that keep ravens away.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: For example, the cubit of spikes that drives away ravens.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף answers the question with a real example of a noticeable item.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The spikes on the roof are a separate, visible fixture that anyone can see and point to. That makes them 'noticeable', so they may not be taken from a גוי even after the building is finished.

keyTerms.meaning: For example
A cubit of spikes that keeps away ravens. Literally, 'a cubit that destroys the raven'.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
For example, the cubit that drives away ravens.
phrases.notes: These were sharp spikes, a cubit long, on the roof of the היכל so birds could not land there.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף: כְּגוֹן אַמָּה כָּלְיָא עוֹרֵב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 4.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A noticeable item is something like the raven-repelling spikes on the roof.

steps.title: Challenge from נחמיה's letter to the king
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף challenges the rule that nothing is accepted at the beginning: נחמיה asked a non-Jewish king for wood to build.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף raised an objection: 'And a letter to Asaf, the keeper of the king's forest...' (so that he would give wood for the building).
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף attacks the 'beginning' rule using a פסוק where נחמיה asks the Persian king for building materials.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the second בית המקדש was being built, which is the beginning stage, נחמיה asked a non-Jewish king to supply wood. According to רבי יוחנן, nothing at all should be taken from non-Jews at that stage. So how could they take wood?

keyTerms.meaning: A letter
An orchard or forest, here the king's wooded park
And so on. The rest of the פסוק is assumed.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef raised an objection:
'And a letter to Asaf,
phrases.notes: נחמיה 2:8. The rest of the פסוק asks Asaf to give wood for building, which is the real point of the challenge.

phrases.english: the keeper of the king's forest,' and so on.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the 'beginning' rule of steps 2-3 and challenges it.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's rule that nothing is accepted from non-Jews at the beginning of building
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: נחמיה took wood from a non-Jewish king while the building was just starting, which goes against that rule.

steps.title: A government is different
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers that a king's government is different because it does not go back on its word.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: A government is different, since it does not go back on its word.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי defends רבי יוחנן's rule by showing that the case in נחמיה is a special exception.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule against taking from non-Jews at the beginning still holds. A royal government is an exception because, once it promises something, it never takes it back. The fact that this is the difference hints that the usual worry is a private donor backing out partway.

keyTerms.meaning: It is different. Used to set a case apart as an exception.
The government or kingdom
Goes back on it, retracts

phrases.english: Abaye said to him:
A government is different,
since it does not go back on its word,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב יוסף's challenge in step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Making a distinction: a government is an exception
steps.terutzHavaAmina: נחמיה's request seemed to show that taking from non-Jews at the beginning is allowed.
steps.terutzMaskana: The general rule stays. A royal government is an exception because it does not retract.

steps.title: שמואל: a government that says it will uproot mountains does it
steps.stepSummary: אביי supports his point with שמואל's saying that a government carries out even huge promises without backing down.
steps.simpleTranslation: As שמואל said: If the government says 'I will uproot mountains', it uproots mountains and does not go back on its word.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי brings שמואל's saying as proof that a government keeps its word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל's picture is extreme on purpose: even something as hard as moving mountains, a government will do once it has said so. This supports אביי's claim that a king's promise can be relied on, unlike a private person's. That is why accepting from the Persian king was acceptable.

keyTerms.meaning: I will uproot mountains
And does not retract it

steps.whatToRemember: At the beginning of building, nothing is taken from non-Jews, not even water and salt. At the end, only items that do not stand out are taken. A king's government is an exception because it never backs out of its promise.

phrases.english: As Shmuel said:
If the government says 'I will uproot mountains,'
it uproots mountains and does not go back on it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports אביי's answer in step 7.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that a government does not retract

steps.title: A non-Jew who separates תרומה
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה quotes רב: when a non-Jew separates תרומה, we check his intent. With a Jew's intent, it goes to a כהן. Otherwise it needs גניזה, since he may have meant it for Heaven.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: If a non-Jew separated תרומה from his pile of grain, we check with him. If he separated it with the intent a Jew has, it is given to a כהן. If not, it must be put away, because we worry that in his heart he meant it for Heaven.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic with a rule from רב about תרומה separated by a non-Jew.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A non-Jew may have a different idea of what 'giving to God' means. If he meant it as Jews give תרומה, it is simply given to a כהן. If he possibly meant it for Heaven, meaning the Temple, no one can use it, so it is put away.

keyTerms.meaning: The portion of produce given to a כהן
A pile of threshed grain
With the intent a Jew has
It must be put away (stored or buried, unused)
We are concerned
For Heaven, meaning dedicated to the Temple

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
A non-Jew who separated terumah from his pile of grain,
we check with him.
If he separated it with the intent of a Jew,
it should be given to a kohen;
and if not, it must be put away,
because we worry that perhaps in his heart it was for Heaven.
phrases.notes: 'For Heaven' here means he may have wanted it dedicated to the Temple, not given to a כהן.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic about non-Jews' gifts, after the discussion of a king's promises.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: תרומה separated by a non-Jew goes to a כהן if he had a Jew's intent; otherwise it needs גניזה because of a possible Temple dedication.

steps.title: A beam donated by a non-Jew with God's Name on it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא about a non-Jew who donated a beam with God's Name written on it. With a Jew's intent, the Name is cut off and the rest is used. Otherwise the whole beam needs גניזה.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged from a ברייתא: A non-Jew donated a beam, and God's Name is written on it. We check with him. If he says, 'I set it aside with a Jew's intent,' the Name is cut off and the rest is used. If not, it must be put away, because we worry that in his heart he meant it for Heaven.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a challenge to רב by quoting a ברייתא. The actual question comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא matches רב's rule in structure: check intent, and if he possibly meant it for Heaven, put it away. The one new detail is that God's Name is written on the beam, and the next step builds its challenge on that detail.

keyTerms.meaning: Donated as a voluntary gift
A wooden beam
God's Name
He cuts off (the part with the Name)
The remainder, the rest

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
A non-Jew who donated a beam,
and God's Name is written on it:
we check with him.
If he says, 'I set it aside with the intent of a Jew,'
one cuts off the Name and uses the rest;
and if not, it must be put away,
because we worry that perhaps in his heart it was for Heaven.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא to challenge רב's rule.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's rule that a non-Jew's תרומה needs גניזה if his intent is unclear.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Sets up the source. The attack comes from the detail that the Name is written on the beam.

steps.title: Only the Name causes the need to put it away
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reads the ברייתא closely: the beam needs גניזה only because the Name is on it. That suggests that without the Name, no גניזה is needed, which contradicts רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: The reason it needs to be put away is that the Name is written on it. But if the Name is not written on it, it does not need to be put away!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now states the challenge, drawn from an exact reading of the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the ברייתא mentions the Name, it seems the Name is the reason for גניזה. רב's תרומה has no Name on it, yet he still requires גניזה. So the ברייתא appears to argue with רב.

keyTerms.meaning: The reason is (used to draw an inference)
But in the opposite case (introduces the inference)
It needs, it requires

phrases.english: The reason is that the Name is written on it,
that it needs to be put away;
but if the Name is not written on it,
it does not need to be put away!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the contradiction out of the ברייתא quoted in step 10.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא suggests the Name alone causes גניזה, so an item without a Name, like רב's תרומה, should not need גניזה.

steps.title: Without the Name it also needs to be put away
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that a beam without the Name also needs גניזה. The ברייתא mentions the Name to teach that, with a Jew's intent, only the Name is cut off, because the parts outside the Name are not holy.
steps.simpleTranslation: The same is true even if the Name is not written on it: it also needs to be put away. The ברייתא teaches us this: even though the Name is written on it, one cuts off the Name and uses the rest, because the area that is not where the Name is written is not holy.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב by explaining that the ברייתא mentions the Name for a different reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry that he meant it for Heaven applies with or without a Name, so רב stands. The Name detail is there to teach a new point about the 'Jew's intent' case. We might have thought a Name makes the whole beam unusable, but only the spot where it is written is holy.

keyTerms.meaning: The same law applies
Even though
This is what it comes to teach us
Not in its place (the area outside the Name)

steps.whatToRemember: A non-Jew's gift that may have been meant for Heaven needs גניזה, with or without God's Name on it. When God's Name is on an object, only the spot where it is written is holy.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the Name is what causes גניזה in the 'not a Jew's intent' case. The ברייתא mentions it only to teach that, in the 'Jew's intent' case, the rest of the beam is still usable.

phrases.english: The same is true, that even though
the Name is not written on it,
it also needs to be put away;
and this is what it teaches us:

phrases.aramaic: דְּאַף עַל גַּב דְּשֵׁם כָּתוּב עָלֶיהָ,
phrases.english: that even though the Name is written on it,
one cuts off the Name and uses the rest,
because the part that is not the place of the Name is not holy.

steps.triggerLanguage: הוּא הַדִּין דְּאַף עַל גַּב דְּאֵין שֵׁם כָּתוּב עָלֶיהָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 11 and defends רב.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterprets why the ברייתא mentions a detail: the Name teaches a new point (the rest is usable), not the reason for גניזה.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The Name is the reason the beam needs גניזה, so without it no גניזה is needed.
steps.terutzMaskana: Any uncertain gift for Heaven needs גניזה. The Name teaches that, with a Jew's intent, only the spot of the Name is holy and the rest may be used.

steps.title: Proof that only the Name itself must be cut off
steps.stepSummary: A source from the תנאים supports the answer in step 12: when God's Name is written on vessel handles or bed legs, only the Name is cut off and put in גניזה.
steps.simpleTranslation: As we learned: if God's Name was written on the handles of vessels or on the legs of a bed, one cuts off the Name and puts it in גניזה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a source to back up the answer it just gave about the beam.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 12 said that with a Jew's intent, only the Name is cut off, because the rest of the wood is not holy. This source shows the same rule for ordinary objects. You cut away the Name and hide it, and the rest of the vessel or bed may still be used.

keyTerms.meaning: he cuts off
he hides it away (puts it in גניזה)
handles of vessels
legs of a bed

steps.whatToRemember: Only God's Name itself is holy. The object around it is not, so you cut away the Name and keep using the rest.

phrases.english: As we learned: if it was written
on the handles of vessels
or on the legs of a bed
he must cut it off and hide it away.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source to support the answer in step 12.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that only God's Name is holy, and the material around it is not.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ruling about a Name written on vessel handles and bed legs: cut it off and put it in גניזה.

steps.title: A coin set aside for charity may be used for now
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן quotes רבה בר אבהו: someone who says "this סלע is for צדקה" may change its use, meaning he may use it now and give a different coin later.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said in the name of רבה בר אבהו: one who says "this סלע is for צדקה" is allowed to change it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic: using money that was promised to צדקה before it is handed over.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though he pointed to a specific coin, it does not become untouchable. He may spend it and replace it with another coin of the same value.

keyTerms.meaning: a coin of a certain value
charity
it is allowed to change it (use it and replace it)

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבָהוּ:
phrases.english: Rav Nachman said that Rabba bar Avahu said:
One who says "this sela is for charity"
is allowed to change it.
phrases.notes: He may use this coin now and give charity a different one later.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבָהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: New topic. It moves from holy objects to money set aside for charity.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A coin set aside for צדקה may be used and later replaced.

steps.title: First assumption: only for his own use
steps.stepSummary: People first understood the rule narrowly: he may use the coin for himself, but he may not lend it to someone else.
steps.simpleTranslation: They understood from this: for himself, yes; for someone else, no.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reports how people first read the rule. This sets up the next step, which will reject that reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea was that the permission is limited. The donor himself may borrow from the charity money, but he may not lend it out to others.

keyTerms.meaning: they understood from it (a first assumption)
for himself
for another person

phrases.english: They understood from it:
for himself, yes; for another, no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a first, narrow reading of רבה בר אבהו's rule.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן allows it for others too
steps.stepSummary: רב אמי quotes רבי יוחנן: the coin may be used whether for himself or for someone else.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: רב אמי said in the name of רבי יוחנן: whether for himself or for another.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings רבי יוחנן's statement, which rejects the narrow reading from step 15.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 15 assumed he may use the coin only for himself. רבי יוחנן says he may also lend it to others, so the permission is broad.

keyTerms.meaning: whether for himself or for another

phrases.aramaic: אִיתְּמַר: אָמַר רַב אַמֵּי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: It was stated: Rav Ami said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
Whether for himself or for another.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיתְּמַר: אָמַר רַב אַמֵּי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the narrow assumption of step 15.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The assumption that the coin may be used only for oneself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: רבי יוחנן explicitly allows lending it to others as well.

steps.title: רבי זעירא: the rule applies only when he said "upon me"
steps.stepSummary: רבי זעירא limits the rule. If he said "עלי" (I am obligated to give), he may use the coin. If he said "הרי זו" (this coin is charity), he must give that very coin.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זעירא said: they taught this only when he said "upon me." But if he said "this one is," he must give it exactly as it is.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זעירא adds a limit: the permission to use the coin depends on how the person worded his pledge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying "עלי" creates a personal debt, so any coin can pay it off. Saying "הרי זו" points to a specific coin. רבי זעירא holds that this ties the pledge to that coin, so he may not swap it.

keyTerms.meaning: they only taught this in the case of
"upon me": a personal obligation to give
"this one is": pointing to a specific item
as it is, itself

steps.confusionAlert: Keep the two wordings straight. "עלי" means "I owe a סלע." "הרי זו" means "this specific coin is charity."

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira said: They only taught
where he said "upon me,"
but if he said "this one is"
he must give it as it is.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי זְעֵירָא: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows רבה בר אבהו's rule to one type of wording.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Using the coin is allowed only with the wording "עלי". With "הרי זו" the coin must be given as is.

steps.title: רבא: the reverse makes more sense
steps.stepSummary: רבא argues that with "זו" it is better to let him use the coin, because that makes him responsible for it. With "עלי" there is no such reason.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא challenged it: On the contrary, the reverse makes sense. If he said "this one," he may use it, so that he becomes responsible for it. But if he said "upon me," no!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks רבי זעירא's distinction and argues it should be flipped.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he said "זו" and the coin got lost, he would not have to replace it. Once he uses it, he becomes responsible to pay it back, which helps the poor. With "עלי" he already owes a סלע no matter what, so using the coin gains charity nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: challenged it
on the contrary
the reverse is more logical
responsibility for loss

phrases.english: Rava challenged it:
On the contrary, the reverse makes sense
if he said "this one," he may use it,
so that he becomes responsible for it,
but if he said "upon me," no!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רָבָא: אַדְּרַבָּה, אִיפְּכָא מִיסְתַּבְּרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי זעירא's distinction in step 17.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי זעירא's claim that only "עלי" allows using the coin.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: With "זו" there is a real benefit to using the coin, because the donor becomes responsible for it. With "עלי" he is responsible anyway, so the logic points the opposite way.

steps.title: Conclusion: no difference between the wordings
steps.stepSummary: רבא ends his challenge by concluding that there is no difference: in both cases he may use the coin.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, there is no difference.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא finishes his argument. He drops רבי זעירא's distinction and rules that the wording makes no difference.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since each wording has its own reason to allow using the coin, neither one is stricter. Whether he said "עלי" or "הרי זו", he may use the coin and replace it.

keyTerms.meaning: there is no difference

steps.whatToRemember: A person who pledges a coin to צדקה may use it and replace it, for himself or for others. It makes no difference whether he said "עלי" or "הרי זו".

phrases.english: Rather, there is no difference.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רבא's challenge in step 18. Since each wording has a reason to allow using the coin, רבא concludes that both are the same.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Both wordings allow using the pledged coin and replacing it later.

steps.title: A ברייתא that supports רבא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא in line with רבא: 'A נדר is צדקה, but הקדש is not צדקה.'
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in line with רבא: A vow is charity, but consecrated property is not charity.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to back up רבא's view. Its wording is unclear, so the next steps will explain it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא held that a person may use a coin he set aside for צדקה, even if he said 'הרי זו'. This ברייתא compares צדקה to נדר and to הקדש. The proof only becomes clear once its wording is explained.

keyTerms.meaning: in line with him; supporting his view
a vow to give something
property set aside for the בית המקדש
charity

phrases.english: It was taught in a ברייתא in line with רבא:
phrases.notes: רבא is the one from Step 18, who said a person may use the coin even when he said 'this coin'.

phrases.english: A vow is charity,
but consecrated property is not charity.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source that supports רבא's position and the conclusion in Step 19.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's view that a coin set aside for צדקה may be used, even after saying 'הרי זו'.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא: נדר צדקה ואין הקדש צדקה.

steps.title: The ברייתא's wording makes no sense as it stands
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the ברייתא means, since neither a נדר nor הקדש is actually צדקה.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is it saying? Neither a vow nor consecrated property is charity!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that, read literally, the ברייתא makes no sense. This sets up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A נדר is a vow and הקדש belongs to the מקדש. Neither one is the same thing as צדקה. So the ברייתא cannot mean that one 'is' צדקה and the other is not, and it must be read in a different way.

keyTerms.meaning: what is it saying? (the wording is unclear)

phrases.english: What is it saying?
Neither a vow nor consecrated property is charity!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the literal meaning of the ברייתא just quoted.
steps.kashyaTarget: The wording 'נדר צדקה ואין הקדש צדקה'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Read literally, the statement is impossible, because neither a נדר nor הקדש is identical with צדקה.

steps.title: צדקה is like a נדר for timing, but unlike הקדש for use
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא means that צדקה falls under בל תאחר like a נדר, but unlike הקדש it may be used. This supports רבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, isn't this what it means: Charity is subject to 'do not delay' like a vow, but it is not like consecrated property. Consecrated property may not be used, while charity may be used.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what the ברייתא really means. That explanation completes the proof for רבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: צדקה is like a נדר in one way: he must give it on time, or he breaks בל תאחר. It is unlike הקדש in another way: using הקדש is forbidden, but using צדקה money is allowed. The ברייתא makes no difference between 'עלי' and 'הרי זו', so it allows use in both cases, just as רבא held.

keyTerms.meaning: rather, isn't it so that... (introduces the forced reading)
the prohibition against delaying the fulfillment of a vow
forbidden to make use of
permitted

steps.whatToRemember: צדקה is like a נדר because he must not delay giving it. It is not like הקדש, because he may use the money in the meantime.
steps.confusionAlert: Being allowed to use the coin does not mean he may hold back the צדקה. He still has to give the amount on time because of בל תאחר.

phrases.english: Rather, isn't this what it is saying:
charity is subject to 'do not delay,'
phrases.notes: This is from the פסוק about vows in דברים 23:22.

phrases.english: but it is not like consecrated property,
for consecrated property is forbidden to be used,
while charity is permitted to be used.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the difficulty in Step 21 by rereading the ברייתא, which completes the proof begun in Step 20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the text: the ברייתא compares צדקה to נדר and to הקדש in specific ways.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to say that a נדר literally is צדקה.
steps.terutzMaskana: צדקה shares בל תאחר with a נדר, but unlike הקדש it may be used in every case.

steps.title: רב זביד's version: the full rule comes from רב
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד from נהרדעא learned the whole ruling in רב's name: the coin may be switched for himself or for others, whether he said 'עלי' or 'הרי זו'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא said: I said this teaching before רב זביד from נהרדעא. He said: You learn it this way; we learn it this way. רב נחמן said in the name of רבה בר אבוה in the name of רב: One who says 'this coin is for charity' may switch it, whether for himself or for another, whether he said 'upon me' or 'this coin.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא reports a different version of the earlier discussion. In this version, every detail is part of the original ruling of רב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the version learned so far, the rule was first understood narrowly and then widened step by step through the discussion. In רב זביד's version, רב himself said everything at once: for himself or for others, with 'עלי' or with 'הרי זו'. The final ruling stays the same, but now it rests on an earlier source.

keyTerms.meaning: a teaching or ruling, together with its discussion
you learn it / we learn it (versions of a teaching)
to switch it (to use it and give a different coin instead)
'upon me': a personal obligation to give
'this one is': setting aside this specific coin

steps.whatToRemember: In רב זביד's version, רב himself allowed switching a צדקה coin in every case: for himself or others, with 'עלי' or 'הרי זו'.

phrases.english: רב כהנא said:
I said this teaching
phrases.notes: He means רב נחמן's ruling about the צדקה coin, with the whole back-and-forth that followed it.

phrases.english: before רב זביד of נהרדעא,
he said: You learn it this way,
we learn it this way —

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבוּהּ אָמַר רַב:

One who says, 'This coin is for charity,'

steps.triggerLanguage: אַתּוּן הָכִי מַתְנִיתוּ לַהּ, אֲנַן הָכִי מַתְנֵינַן לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives another version of the whole discussion from Steps 14-19, with the full rule credited to רב.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A coin set aside for צדקה may be switched in all cases: for himself or for others, with 'עלי' or with 'הרי זו'.

steps.title: Once the גבאי has the coin, it may not be switched
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that he may switch the צדקה coin only until it reaches the גבאי צדקה. After that, switching is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: 'This coin is for charity.' Before it reaches the hands of the charity collector, he may switch it. Once it reaches the hands of the charity collector, he may not switch it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא that limits the permission to switch a צדקה coin.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everything so far allowed the owner to switch the coin. This ברייתא adds a time limit. The permission lasts only while the coin is still with him. Once the גבאי receives it, the coin may no longer be switched.

keyTerms.meaning: charity collector, appointed to gather and hand out צדקה
before it came into the hands of
from the time it came

steps.whatToRemember: He may switch a צדקה coin only while it is still with him. Once the גבאי has received it, switching is forbidden.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the practical limit on the permission discussed so far. The freedom to use צדקה money ends once the money reaches the גבאי.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: 'This coin is for charity' —
before it has come into the hands of the charity collector,
it is permitted to switch it;
once it has come into the hands of the charity collector,
it is forbidden to switch it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a limit to the permission just stated: it applies only before the coin reaches the גבאי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Switching a צדקה coin is allowed before it reaches the גבאי and forbidden once it does.
